en: The Buddha Spoke the Sūtra on the Greatness of the Buddha and the Greatness of the Saṃgha, translated by the lay devotee Juqu Jingsheng of the Song Dynasty.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Rājagṛha. In that kingdom there was a wealthy man named Lei, who possessed vast quantities of gold and silver.
His treasures, fields, houses, oxen, horses, and male and female slaves were beyond counting.
As he grew old in his later years, he had no heirs whatsoever.
According to the established law of that country, the property of anyone who dies without a son is entirely confiscated by the state.

He offered fervent prayers to the sun and moon, the various heavens, ghosts, and spirits, as well as the Nine Sons’ Mother and the deities of mountains and trees, entreating them all for a son, yet he was unable to obtain one.
Li thought to himself:

"Whenever people face urgent distress, they invariably go to seek refuge with the spirits of the mountains and trees, yet there is nothing these spirits can do for them—wealth and treasures vanish, their livelihoods fall into ruin, illnesses follow one after another, calamities strike from head to tail, servants and slaves die, and the six domestic animals fail to breed—all because of these malevolent omens."

The spirits and deities, their guides, have become deluded and cause them to dance; they dwell within the hearts of chaotic rulers, claiming that blessings are imminent when calamities instead descend heavily. This is like a blind man swallowing poison while calling it a wholesome medicine, hoping for recovery, yet the poison taking hold and destroying his life.
"Now I kill living beings to sacrifice to the spirits and deities, yet I hope for heavenly blessings while destined for hell—is this not delusion?
In the world there is the Way of the Buddha, with sages of lofty conduct; there are those who attain immortality, known as the True Persons (Arhats)."

The True Person is pure, like a lapis lazuli bead; only through diligent cultivation and focused contemplation can one behold them. Those who uphold this Way maintain only tranquility and stillness, being without desire or seeking, taking this as their joy; they attain peace in the present life and, at the end of their lives, are reborn in the heavens.
Li thought to herself:
"Setting aside my regular offerings, I shall serve the Buddha and the Triple Gem.
After she had served the Buddha for one year, her wife gave birth to a son, whereupon Li said:
"By serving the Buddha, I have obtained this boon; let his name be Buddhada. As for the Buddha’s disciples, they are titled Bhikṣusaṃgha.
He then served [the Buddha] once more, and before a full year had passed, another worthy son was born, whose name was Saṃghada.
Li instructed his two sons, demonstrating to them the Way of the Sages.

Sengda was by nature benevolent toward all beings; his filial piety was unsurpassed. He recited the Buddhist precepts, drew near to śramaṇas, and lived with purity and contentment. Having personally witnessed his resolve, Li held him in exceptional affection.
When his father was stricken with illness and confined to bed, he immediately summoned his eldest son and, weeping, instructed him:

"All who are born must die; all things are impermanent. Those who uphold the precepts find peace; those who violate them face peril. By upholding the Buddha’s precepts, one remains free from affliction from beginning to end."
"Sengda is still young, yet he is benevolent, filial, and pure... After Li had repeated these words many times, just as the phrasing was finished, he suddenly passed away.
Having lost his father, Sengda was left orphaned with no one to turn to for guidance; he repeatedly petitioned his elder brother, saying, "I wish to become a śramaṇa."
According to the custom of that country, when a man wished to seek a wife, he would feign and falsely say,
"I wish to become a śramaṇa.
Fearing this might actually happen, his relatives would immediately arrange a marriage for him.

The Buddha, considering his younger brother to be of a similar deceptive nature, immediately sought out the daughter of the most virtuous family in the kingdom, named Kṣemadarsinī. Her radiance was brilliant and magnificent; she was upright and peerless, with height, weight, and build perfectly proportioned. Pure, compassionate, and filial, she was like the moon among the stars; there was no noble lady or virtuous wife in the kingdom who did not praise and rejoice in her.
When the wife returned and ascended the hall, and the elder brother gathered his guests, the nine branches of the clan were all joyful and lived in harmony.
To the assembled guests, the elder brother addressed his younger brother, saying:
"On this day, would it be appropriate for you to become a śramaṇa?"
The Elder replied, "Elder brother!
To release me so that I may become a śramaṇa is truly my long-cherished wish."
When the elder brother awoke, Heaven, desiring to test him, teased him, saying, "You may follow your own wishes.
The younger brother’s heart was filled with joy; he paid homage to his elder brother and entered the mountains that very day.
He saw a śramaṇa, young and handsome, dwelling alone beneath a tree; he approached him, joined his palms, bowed his head in salutation, and stepping back, asked:
"Virtuous one, for what reason have you gone forth to become a śramaṇa?"
That person, having already attained the path of Arhatship and possessing foreknowledge of events throughout countless kalpas past and future, said to Saṃghadatta:
"The Buddha’s sutras state:
'A person who indulges in lust is like one whose body is being consumed by fire, or like one carrying a torch while walking against the wind.'"

If the flame recedes slightly and one does not let go of the torch, the fire will burn one's hand; it is like a crow holding meat while hawks and falcons pursue and scramble for it—if the crow does not let go of the meat, disaster will befall its own life.
"Immoral lust such as this brings nothing but peril; it is for this reason that I have become a śramaṇa.
It is like a sharp blade smeared with honey: a child, craving the sweetness, licks it with its tongue and suffers the calamity of having its tongue cut off."
Those who are lewd and dissolute merely seek to gratify their foolish minds, failing to consider that they will later suffer the calamity of having their bodies burned.

It is like a starving dog that finds a dry bone on the road; it gnaws and bites at it until its mouth is wounded and its teeth broken. This only brings injury and ruin upon itself—what benefit does it bring to the dog?
"With such lewdness as this, for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas there will not be even a hair’s breadth of merit, but only the sins of the three miserable realms.
It is because I contemplate this that I have become a śramaṇa."

It is like a tree with abundant flowers and fruit; when a traveler covets them and strikes them with a staff or stone, in an instant the flowers are damaged, the fruit falls, and the branches and leaves are mangled.
A tree, by means of its flowers and fruits, invites its own withering and destruction;
a moth, greedy for the color of fire, throws itself into a lamp, its body scorched and cooked—what can it possibly gain thereby?

Those who are deluded by lust cannot distinguish between good and evil; they distance themselves from the worthy and draw near to the foolish. Day by day they sink into darkness, leading to the ruin of their state and the destruction of their people. Upon death, they enter hell; when their wickedness is manifest and their transgressions complete, what can be done when it is too late for regret?
The Buddha beheld this truth and revealed the noble path.

Relying on the Buddha’s grace, I have been able to behold the sutras and precepts; guarding my mind in purity, I remain solitary and free from affliction. Looking back upon the worldly customs, I realize they were but errors.
"It is for this reason that I have become a śramaṇa.
When Sengda heard this, he prostrated himself at his feet, knelt for a long time, and said:
"The Buddha is truly a supreme sage, the most honored among all the devas!"
The Sūtra, which extinguishes delusion, has entered my heart.
I vow to leave behind the turbidity of the world and tread the path of purity, upholding the precepts of a śramaṇa as my honor and blessing.
The Master then instructed him on the grave precepts of a śramaṇa.
After attending his teacher for several months, he addressed the Master, saying:
"For what reason do you wish to enter the mountain wilderness to practice silent concentration and meditative rest, seeking the Way of Arhatship, so as to extinguish all afflictions?"
The Master said:
"To dwell alone in the mountains is a great hardship.
One who dwells in the mountains and marshes should study the constellations to clearly understand the seasons, and should always store water, fire, parched grain, and honey."

The reason for this is that when bandits seek water, fire, parched grain, or honey at midnight or toward dawn, they demand that these be provided; if one fails to give them what they desire, the bandits will invariably kill the person.
Sengda replied: "Yes!
I respectfully receive your compassionate instruction and shall fully study what you have commanded."
He then entered the mountains.
His elder brother thought to himself:
"My younger brother has become a śramaṇa; he will certainly never maintain a wife."
His wife, Kāśisundarī, was peerlessly beautiful; her brother took a liking to her and rose to follow her. Taking his lute with him, he struck poses and played it while singing a licentious song:
"The radiant saffron flower grows in the wild fields; if not gathered when its time has passed, it is left cast aside."
Your countenance is radiant and flourishing, your complexion fresh and new; share this joy with me, for we are indeed close kin. Once you have grown old in years, who would cherish you so?
Kāśyapa immediately perceived that his elder brother intended to cause a disturbance; he then responded to the Buddha with a song, saying:
"Sublime is my Teacher, the Honored One of gods and men; his disciples are pure, and are thus titled *śramaṇas*."
I praise the truth as being sacred and lust as belonging to the realm of beasts.
Having received the solemn precepts, I shall not serve two masters; I will never engage in lustful conduct throughout my life, even at the cost of my own life.
The Buddha sang a song of profound compassion with plaintive words: "My long-cherished heart has been set upon you;
therefore, through a worthy matchmaker, I inquired after your name and sought a master to divine an auspicious time.
I was sorrowful and anxious, fearing you would not come; now that I behold your radiant countenance, my heart is filled with joy."
"If we do not unite in joy now, would it not be a mere waste?
This vow is settled; why should the noble lady have any doubt?
Kāśyapa was filled with trepidation and replied in song:

“The Buddha established rites and ceremonies so that the distinctions between the honorable and the humble are maintained: a younger brother’s wife is like one’s own son, while a husband’s elder brother is like one’s own father.
I personally uphold the precepts with daily increasing vigor; I am truly equal to the sages, whereas lust is but the behavior of insects and rats.”
"Alas, Elder Brother!
Why do you speak such words?
The elder brother’s mind was bewildered; his craving for a quick and pleasing vision was so extreme that it could not be turned away.
Kuaijian also sang:
"When a person lives in this world, they should keep two things at a distance:
filial impiety and lewd disorder."
"Your conduct violates the Buddha's precepts; both gods and sages note your distinctiveness.
The Buddha sang this great song:

"Your countenance is so radiant and bright; among all the beautiful women in heaven, who could possess such a face? My heart is filled with delight, and thus I have crossed the great mountains to reach you."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This man desires me; his perverse madness will lead to great calamity.
I shall describe the impurities and foul secretions within my own body, and only then will he desist."
Kuaijian replied gravely:
"If you covet my body, what is so good about it?
It consists of nine bones joined together as a skull, within which there is nothing but brain matter; the face has seven apertures from which mucus and saliva flow."
It is skin wrapping bone; for those who crave the head and neck, there is skin and flesh wrapped together, with body hair and bristles, nails, teeth, skin, and muscle, blood, brain, bone, and marrow;
within the abdomen are the heart, spleen, kidneys, intestines, and stomach, along with fat, lungs, excrement, urine, pus, blood, chills, and fevers;

the feet are connected to the calves, the calves to the thighs, the thighs to the buttocks, the buttocks to the waist, the waist to the spine, the spine to the ribs, the ribs to the neck, the neck to the skull, the arms to the elbows, and the elbows to the shoulders.
I am like a painted vase filled with excrement and urine; the impurities within my body are as loathsome as this—how could they be an object of craving?
Regarding whatever ordinary people find pleasing, if one speaks of its foulness, their minds immediately despise it.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"The woman is so preoccupied with her husband that how could she possibly heed my words?
Only if I kill her brother will she comply."
The Buddha, filled with great indignation, immediately went out to recruit several former bandits.
Seeing some frivolous men at a wine shop, he approached them and said:
"Do you know that the six domestic slaves kept in my household have fled to become śramaṇas; they are currently in the mountains."
The bandits said,
"We know you. Mahāgovinda immediately took out gold and silver and gave it to them, ordering them to kill his slave boy.
"Quickly take back his head, the upper garment upon his body, the Dharma-staff he held, and the sandals upon his feet; I shall further bestow gold and silver upon you all."
The bandit was greatly pleased and said,
"Take as much as you wish from me.
He then departed and entered the mountains.
He went to his younger brother's place and called out,
"Śramaṇa! Come out quickly!"
His younger brother came out and said,
"What do you seek, gentlemen?
I have water and fire, and parched grain with honey for you to eat."
When midnight had passed, the bandits said, "We do not seek water, fire, parched grain, or honey; we do not ask for your time. We merely wish to take your head with us."
Upon hearing this, his younger brother was immediately seized with great terror and, weeping, said:
"I am not the son of a wealthy man or a feudal lord!

Having renounced the secular world for the Way, I have no quarrels with the world; my study of the Way has been brief, and I have not yet attained the stages of Stream-winner, Once-returner, Non-returner, Arhat, or the six supernormal powers. What benefit would there be in killing me?"
The bandit said, "I have come for the sake of your head; your empty lamentations are of no avail—what benefit is there in seeking mercy?
His younger brother thought to himself:
"This thief alone has heard that I am from a wealthy family, and he thinks I must have brought treasures here.

He said to the thief, "If you wish to obtain treasures, my elder brother is at home; his name is Buddhada. Send him a letter to bestow treasures upon you, so that you may obtain whatever you desire according to your own wishes."
The robber said,
"Your elder brother sent me here to kill you.
His younger brother replied:
"It is because of this woman that I am now dying.
Previously, my teacher warned me:
'When a person dwells with a paramour, it is like holding a torch against the wind; if one does not cast it aside early, the fire will surely burn one's hand.'"
Like a blade smeared with honey, like a hawk pursuing a crow, a dog gnawing at a dry bone, or the flowers and fruits of a tree—
form is a source of harm to the body, as profound as a teacher’s admonition.
Weeping, he followed the bandits, saying:
"I beg for one more year of life so that I may attain the Way.
I shall always remain here; it will not be long before you kill me."
The bandit said, "I now wish to take your head; why do you speak of one year?
Many practitioners who dwell in the mountains have attained the Way; I fear that you might lightly display your supernatural powers and depart."
"Do not say more; take my head and go.
His younger brother spoke again, saying, "I pray that you do not kill me immediately, but first cut off one of my thighs and place it before me."
The thief then stepped forward and first severed one of his thighs, placing it before him.
As his younger brother suffered this agony beyond description, a deva descended from heaven to the place where the practitioner was and said:
"Do not be afraid; hold fast to your mind."
In your previous lives, you entered among the animals, where people slaughtered and carved you to sell your flesh; this has not been for just one lifetime.
You have undergone the realms of hell and hungry ghosts; your experience of suffering has not begun only now.
Sengda said to the deity:
"Please speak with compassion to my teacher so that he may know: because of my teacher’s instruction in the Way, I have come to realize where birth and death truly lie."
The deity immediately went and spoke to his teacher, saying:
"Your worthy disciple wishes to see you; people wish to kill him, and he has wept and entreated with piteous cries."
The Master flew through the air to where his disciple was and preached the sutra for him, saying:
"Heaven and earth and Mount Sumeru shall yet perish; the oceans shall dry up; and all shall be destroyed by the seven suns."

When wind arises over the world, it is called *lán*; once this *lán* wind begins, mountain after mountain collides with one another, yet even this wind eventually ceases—how much more so for your tiny body? What comparison can there possibly be?
One should simply practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

The Buddha has always taught that all things are impermanent: that which flourishes must inevitably decline; that meeting is followed by separation; and that positions of honor and rank are difficult to preserve—the human body is no different.
When the monk defecated, he attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);
when his other thigh was severed, as he again recollected his teacher’s precepts, he attained the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*);
when the bandits severed his left hand, as he again recollected his teacher’s precepts, he attained the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The bandit severed his right hand, yet he again recollected the precepts of his teacher and attained the path of Arhatship;
he thus no longer feared the three evil realms, attaining mastery over birth and death, with nothing further to fear.
Sengda said, "Bring me some tree bark.
He immediately peeled off some tree bark and gave it to him.
Sengda took a branch to make a brush, pierced his own body to draw blood, and wrote upon the bark of a tree:
"Elder Brother!
Are you well and at ease according to the seasons?"
"While my two parents were still alive, I entrusted you, my elder brother, with their care.
You did not honor this trust, but instead violated and abandoned their instructions; for the sake of female beauty, we have come to such a state where kinsmen slaughter one another."
To disobey the compassionate instructions of one's parents is unfilial;
to cruelly kill human life is unkind.
The sin of killing a single animal is no small matter, let alone killing an Arhat.
I have not ceased my practice; it is you, elder brother, who have invited this upon yourself.
You think that because I possess a physical form, I can be killed;
yet the Sugata is tranquil and silent—your mutual harm is in vain.
"May we be long parted; strive diligently and aspire to honor the True Way.
He extended his neck by two feet and said to the bandit, "When you sever my head, it will be like cutting through mud; do not harbor any fear."
"I fear you will fall into hell.

The robber stepped forward, severed his head, and took from his body the robes, staff, sandals, and bowl. He carried these to his elder brother; he gave the robes, staff, sandals, and bowl all to his brother, who then rewarded the robber with a heavy gift of gold and silver.

The elder brother took his younger brother’s head, fashioned a lifelike form, and placed the head upon it; he dressed it in clothes and set the staff, bowl, and sandals beside it, saying to Kṣema-darśana:
"Your husband has returned home; you may go to greet him."
Kuaijian was greatly delighted and ran to where he was; seeing him sitting with his eyes closed, she thought he was contemplating the Way and did not dare call out to him.
She prepared various fine foods, thinking to herself:
"When he awakens, I shall feed him."
At midday he did not wake up, so his wife approached him and said, "It is now midday; I fear we have passed the proper time.

Wondrously surprised that he did not respond, she pulled at his robe to rouse him, whereupon his head fell to the ground and his body was completely dismembered, with each part lying in a different direction.
The wife was immediately seized with great terror;
she threw herself on the ground, leaping up and down, and cried out, "Has my son finally brought this upon himself?
Shall I witness such a cruel atrocity! In her grief and indignation, she called out to Heaven; her liver and heart were rent asunder, blood gushed from her mouth, and she died suddenly.

His conduct of the precepts is pure and white, as difficult to defile as space; he has established his mind upon the model of the sages, as difficult to move as the earth; his steadfast and pure practice is lofty, as difficult to fathom as heaven.
Before his life had ended, the devas sighed in admiration; they pre-emptively secured his place of rebirth and welcomed his spirit to dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
By enduring a moment of lust, he obtained celestial glory that is inexhaustible.

The elder brother entered the spirit chamber to see what had become of his wife; he saw his younger brother’s head and body scattered in a chaotic mess, while his wife lay dead on one side, vomiting blood.
Seeing his younger brother’s wife’s corpse in such a state, the elder brother cried out: "Alas! Alas!"
"I have gone against the Way of Heaven, and my deeds were so cruel and violent that they have led me to this state.
The elder brother immediately went to the place where the bandits were and asked their intention:
"Does my younger brother have any final words as he approaches death?"
The bandit said,
"I have a letter," and showed it to him.
The words of the letter were earnest and poignant; having finished reading it, my five internal organs were choked with grief, and tears flowed profusely as they crossed one another:

"I have defied the compassionate instructions of my honored parents at their deathbeds; I have caused the slaughter of my own kin and further killed an Arhat. Moved by such remorse, I shall die, and upon death, I shall enter hell."

When the king, his ministers, and the common people heard of this tragic event, they wiped away their tears and choked with sobs; they extolled his pure virtue and performed the funeral rites for his younger brother.
The fourfold assembly erected a stupa, while devas, nāgas, and spirits filled the air, scattering flowers and burning incense—all were moved by grief.

Her husband, Kuàijiàn, was buried by the people of the state; their collective mourning shook the nation, and all under heaven praised him. Through his diligent cultivation, he attained the Way; without violating the five precepts, he remained chaste and was reborn in the heavens.
Violating the teachings of the Buddha, being unfilial and harming the sages, they shall die and enter hell, where they will suffer the bitter torment of burning and boiling for years beyond counting.
The Buddha then addressed his disciples, instructing them to exhort one another with renewed diligence to remain free from desire.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the disciples rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
This concludes the Sutra on the Greatness of the Buddha and the Greatness of the Sangha.
